title: PIRATE Act
official_summary:
Preventing Illegal Radio Abuse Through Enforcement Act or the PIRATE Act

This bill addresses unlicensed radio broadcasting (called pirating), including by increasing the maximum fine for a pirate radio broadcasting violation to $2 million and imposing a fine of up to $100,000 per day for pirating violations subject to the $2 million limit.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) must (1) annually submit to Congress a report summarizing implementation of this bill and associated enforcement activities for the previous fiscal year; and (2) at least once a year, assign appropriate enforcement personnel to focus specific and sustained attention on the elimination of pirate radio broadcasting within the top five radio markets.

The FCC may not preempt any state or local law prohibiting pirate radio broadcasting.

The FCC shall (1) revise its rules to require that, absent good cause, in any case alleging a violation, it shall proceed directly to issue a Notice of Apparent Liability without first issuing a Notice of Unlicensed Operation; and (2) publish a database of all licensed radio stations operating in the AM and FM band that includes each licensed station and all entities that have received a Notice of Unlicensed Operation, Notice of Apparent Liability, or Forfeiture Order issued by the FCC.

summary.headline: A 2020 law raises fines for unlicensed radio broadcasting and requires the FCC to crack down on pirate radio more directly.
summary.what_it_does: The law raises the maximum fine for pirate radio broadcasting to $2 million and allows fines of up to $100,000 per day for violations under that limit. It requires the FCC to skip a warning step in most cases and go straight to a Notice of Apparent Liability, unless there is good cause. The FCC must also assign enforcement staff to focus on pirate radio in the top five radio markets each year, and it must publish a public database of licensed AM and FM stations and entities that received FCC enforcement notices. The FCC cannot block state or local laws against pirate radio, and it must send Congress an annual report on enforcement.

who_it_affects.group: People and groups who operate unlicensed radio stations
who_it_affects.how: They face much higher maximum fines and can be penalized more quickly, usually without first receiving a warning notice.

who_it_affects.group: Licensed AM and FM radio station owners
who_it_affects.how: Their station information is listed in a public FCC database that also shows entities that have received enforcement notices.

who_it_affects.group: Residents of the top five radio markets
who_it_affects.how: The FCC must give sustained enforcement attention to pirate radio in these areas each year.
Their own laws banning pirate radio cannot be overridden by the FCC.

summary.when_it_takes_effect: The law took effect when it was enacted on January 24, 2020, though the FCC must revise its rules and publish the database afterward, and the exact timing of those steps is not stated in the summary.
